lines: Windows lets you install apps from anywhere. But outside the Microsoft Store, it's hard to tell who made an app, or whether the file is genuine.
In a survey of sixty Windows users, eighty-seven percent stop or research an app when they don't recognize the publisher.
Windows already has strong protection, but its warnings rarely explain why, and no warning doesn't feel like proof of safety.
So careful people check signatures, compare hashes, or upload files to VirusTotal. Everyone else guesses.
People weren't asking whether a file was signed.
They were asking who made it.
So I split trust into two questions. Is the developer verified, with an identity that follows them across apps and releases?
And is this exact file signed, unchanged, and recognized? Security signals fill in the rest, so signed never has to mean safe.
Instead of block or allow, I designed four states. A trusted app from a verified developer installs after a short countdown.
A signed app from an unverified developer gets a plain explanation and a choice. An unsigned app gets the strongest warning, and a new version from a known developer sits in between.
A warning alone leaves people stuck, so the experience also points to the Microsoft Store.
It looks for the same app from the same publisher first. When there isn't one, AI suggests a verified alternative.
To test it on real installers, I built a working Windows app with AI. It runs when a setup file starts, or from the right-click menu.
Each scan combines six checks, from the digital signature to Windows Defender and VirusTotal, in about two seconds, without admin rights.
The trust states went into a pilot in China through Microsoft PC Manager, with more than three hundred thousand trust dialog views across twenty apps.
And the working app showed the whole model holding up on real files.
Trust isn't a badge. It's knowing who made something, and what you're about to run.
